splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing constraints for selecting actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA. The split affected billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year and raises questions about limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be found and punished.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding and the statutory term runs regardless, meaning courts cannot extend the supervisory period beyond what was specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face an additional gatekeeping requirement under § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any prior claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on previously raised claims in § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The split has significant implications for the ease of challenging election rules nationwide and whether such disputes must wait until after an election to be litigated.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate has Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election, recognizing competitive injury from the counting of potentially invalid ballots.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge state ballot-counting rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that carry criminal penalties, such as Sentencing Guidelines enhancements.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in criminal or quasi-criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold lenity prevails, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. Post-Loper Bright, the issue remains significant for Sentencing Guidelines and other criminal regulatory provisions.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to Sentencing Commission commentary prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding conspiracy and attempt to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a permissible interpretation of genuinely ambiguous text or an impermissible expansion beyond the guideline's plain meaning. The split affects thousands of federal drug defendants' sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text is ambiguous as to inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy is entitled to controlling weight as a reasonable interpretation.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond the plain meaning of the guideline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to vastly different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit, implicating fundamental fairness in criminal sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others permit courts to consider them as one factor. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor among others when evaluating compassionate release motions, consistent with the broad discretion granted under the statute.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes categorically cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with state drug convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State schedule suffices
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the particular substance is controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Federal schedule required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if it involves a substance also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether property appreciation occurring between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that held such appreciation belongs to the debtor under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), means post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, consistent with the statute's structure, purpose, and legislative history of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order resolving a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering the shorter 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.citation: See Onamuti (noting minority view in lopsided split)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions affecting the duration or conditions of confinement (such as First Step Act time credit calculations), or whether other remedies like Bivens or the APA are available.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the terms of confinement but do not squarely challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment. The issue affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions on earned time credits, prerelease custody, and other conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy when the challenge goes to the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions on time credits and prerelease custody transfers.

positions.label: Alternative remedies available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as distinct from the fact or duration of imprisonment) may be brought through alternative remedies such as § 1983 or Bivens actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentencing must be limited to the purposes of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation hearings that are expressly punitive in nature. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows courts to punish defendants for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Multiple judges have dissented, arguing this contravenes statutory text and Supreme Court precedent.

positions.label: Punishment permitted at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when revoking supervision and imposing a new term of imprisonment.

positions.label: Punishment not a proper purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should not be based on punishment for the violation but rather on the purposes of supervised release, including deterrence and protection of the public.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: See Esteras dissent noting circuit split

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. The question implicates Spending Clause limits on Congress's power to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds. SCOTUS has taken up the issue.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text clearly authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, or that Congress lacks Spending Clause power to impose such personal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may encompass claims that could also be raised in habeas proceedings under § 2255, such as claims of legal error in the original conviction or sentence. Some circuits permit courts to consider such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a substitute for § 2255.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider claims related to potential errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor among others in the extraordinary-and-compelling-reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use § 3582 as substitute for § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not serve as a vehicle for claims that properly belong under § 2255, and that alleged legal errors in the underlying conviction or sentence are not cognizable as extraordinary and compelling reasons.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
